I won't try to answer the full original rant, as It has been [done very beautifully](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/2173-edgeware-is-not-complicated) by Rich already.
But since I am a bit too often part of RaymondZ's gross whining, I wish to remind some part about point 1 above.
1. Indeed, I "loudly opposed" this funding of 50M EDG for the CW Labs 2020 roadmap, on the basis I found it overpriced and the principle by which it was granted, which was a clear conflict of interest. Note that my personal opposition had no effect since **Commonwealth Labs took over the council with the help of their VC backers at the time** in order to self-granted themselves the funds through a council supermajority. At the time of granting: 50M EDG were equivalent to 1.2M USD for the delivery of the roadmap.
2. Note that the roadmap included deliveries of the EVM we are currently still discussing: from the [official blog](https://blog.edgewa.re/edgeware-2020/) this included benchmarking to define gas prices that we only had very recently. Moreover the same upgrade has been funded [a second time](https://commonwealth.im/edgeware/proposal/discussion/1100-erup-4-substrate-30-evm-updates-runtime-modules) and still isn't properly completed. We cannot throw more money at the same team that failed to deliver despite being generously funded multiple times.
3. CW Labs may have performed a lot, yes. But they took also the vast majority of the funding for this. They have been paid: the chain owes nothing more to teams who just deliver what they are paid for. Arguably, many deliveries are still long overdue (webb mixers paid 7M EDG, EVM as mentioned, etc.), some others have been fraught with operational issues like exchange A lack of communication and 7M EDG (at least) and 25k USD having disappeared from the funding, etc. The question is more about selecting teams that provide the best cost over benefit. So absolute production is not considered in a vacuum. Over time, teams that perform well build a positive reputation and people will be more and more excited and willing to fund them possibly larger amounts. Also the grants part that are not deployed to complete the tasks (since the amounts are always including some bonus part) are already allowing those teams to get more say in governance. Reputation also gives them support from others that would delegate to them. This can be done and we have examples in the council. 
4. The rules above is how partnerships, proposals, etc. should be assessed: Nothing is rejected as long as it is not submitted to a vote, but to expect some significant funding amount, partners ought to be able and willing to expose an ambitious plan and metrics that can prove that the value they create for the chain is greater or equal from the grant they are asking for. This is just basic common sense. How does the value accrue onchain? One example could be through transaction fees for instance. Then we can grant - say - 80% of the fees generated that get sent to the treasury to a project and keep 20% to bootstrap others. This is just an example.

Right now we do have continuing disagreements. 

The reason things feel contentious, is that each side in each situation is speaking from a perspective where they have strong views and cannot understand the other side. 

I've lost count of the times where each side tries to explain their reasoning and the other says words to the effect of 'I don't understand what you are saying', followed by the former getting exasperated and then things get emotional and often retreat into personal attacks.

Some of this definitely has to do with the communication platforms we use - text based messaging remove nuance, asynchornous discussions mean context is easy to lose and hard to follow and ultimately people often speak less kindly to each other when they are not face to face. 

These are however just the conditions that serve to make underlying issues worse, they are not the core challenge itself. 

--------

Above [@raymondz](/edgeware/account/mae7JWE1EEMLcno2ZSB8dahwPqVPEyh8zik6dgNpQTvvucq) outlines his view of where the _fundamental misalignment_** **comes: 

> **Lack of a clarity on what Edgeware is providing as a platform**
> We've presented many different visions for what Edgeware is. An on-chain incubator, a venture community, a smart contract chain for funding media projects — all of these seem like they do not capture the entire picture. 

I think this goes some way, but there is deeper nuance to line that is worth digging into and is basically people disagree on what **a platform is**. 

Lets: start with a definition:

> _A platform is a group of technologies that are used as a base upon which other applications, processes or technologies are developed. - [link](https://www.techopedia.com/definition/3411/platform-computing) _

## **Ethereum as platform **

We can describe **Ethereum** as a platform using this definition - there is a base layer and then apps are built on top, but all have their own L2 native token that accrues value to this main token and because of the massive number of apps, they all use the base token for fees and so this returns value to the platform layer.

This has been the dominant model of Web2 and focuses primarily on web developers, engineers and the generic term 'builders' we hear commonly repeated in and around Edgeware when referring to a particular type of talent.

Let's now see another definition for **platform**. 

> a flat surface that is raised higher than the floor or ground and that people stand on when performing or speaking

## Decred as platform 

Whereas ETH is focused on the issuance of L2 assets, in Decred they are razor focused on **value accrual at L1**, there are no L2 tokens, no ICOs, no abstractions, their view is the biggest opportunity of all is to create 'money'. 

In Decred **money is the platform** and the focus is on creating the most secure, transparent and sustainable system that can fund creative contributions over decades via their governance system. 

Decred exists to fund people, therefore those people need to trust the system and also know that there are no preferential treatment for some contributors, else the system of trust is doomed. 

The most important thing is to ensure the neutrality and accessibility of the systems that would govern and spend this community money... there is no higher goal, this is the purpose and their values are derived from it and they guard it ferociously. 

## Edgeware as platform 

Let's look at the website for Edgeware:

> Edgeware is a smart contract blockchain with a community managed treasury. 

The _smart contract blockchain_ part relates to the Ethereum definiton of a platform.
The _community managed treasury_ relates to the Decred definition of a platform.

These two things are subtly but profoundly different and it is this nuance that causes all of the disagreements, because depending on which side you fall, you frame others behaviour through that lens. 

This is in many ways the current tension in Polkadot/Substrate - with Gavin Wood even recently admitting to [rethinking parachains](https://twitter.com/PAMauric/status/1439963636563423232), as an entirely new thing.

## Commonwealth Labs - ETH as platform reference

The Commonwealth Labs team generally fall on the Ethereum side of the debate. 

The treasury is just a tool to be used to bootstrap apps on L2, with an ETH value accrual model that relies on adoption of said apps, and the community get excited about this because it is also a path to airdrops etc. 

In this version, treasury spending via governance is merely a tool to onboard apps and 'builders' and this leads people to the natural conclusions around offering large % stakes in the network and caring less about the detail around funding and the accusations of nimbyism - per this post. 

In this world view, we waste time worrying about the process, when we should just get funding and so what if the treasury funds projects that might enrich a L2 project and team? 

I can fully understand from this POV why this would seem like nimbyism. 

On the opposing side I definitely fall on into a more Decred worldview, one where  

## Decent Partners - Decred as platform reference

Prior to Edgeware I had spent around 12 months contributing to **Decred which is a blockchain with its own treasury and governance system. **

I spent time trying to understand its technology, rationale and purpose, which was fascinating and brutal in equal measures.

Edgeware is definitely not the only group that argues about governance, or its purpose, or about what things it should fund. My experience concluded with [this post](https://github.com/monsieurbulb/forksintheroad/blob/master/Decred_forks_in_the_road.md) which was written because I felt that Decred was too inward looking, too focused on making hard money, to the detriment of experimenting.

This is what led me to Substrate, to Commonwealth and to Edgeware - because I saw with Substrate there was a system that offered the same basic building blocks as Decred (chain / treasury / governance) and then with the lockdrop, there was a way to ensure a fairly distributed coin that had the chance of becoming a true **community money**, not just a bootstrapping mechanism for L2 apps. 

The irony is, if you read the post, we have many of the same basic issues as Decred. 

This DCR experience and that of my former life in public service broadcasting roots me in not just **what we fund**, but **how we fund **and** why we do it. **

If we don't build trust in the mony narrative, then no-one will accept the money, if we don't ensure everyone is held accountable to the same standards, then what hope do we have of making a fairer system that is open to all, and meritocratic to its core?

## **Edgeware.Agency - ETH/DCR platform reference**

The Edgeware Agency (and [@Thom Ivy](/edgeware/account/jKauGVPCQkteGTDKuuNwhYhMBrj5QuytgybEC4A5cS4Bki5)) are somewhere in the middle and this is where there is a returning tension. At varying points, the agency has been on the ETH side and on the DCR side. 

Have a listen to [his recent podcast](Ramsey (Decentration) — 29/09/2021 https://blockchainrecorded.com/edgeware-blockchain-talk-with-thom-ivy/) - you can hear both sides of the argument and there is now a move towards introducing Edgeware as a Layer 1 DAO (like Decred), since it is a solo chain. 

## Decentration Labs - multi-chain reality 

Just when you thought things were complex enough, we now add another factor to the mix as [@Ramsey](/edgeware/account/k44nJ5yAhFz3XHGeTPuKvegJ4GD1YCSVaPc7wj4miVL6epN) outlines in his [Edgeware a multi-chain reality, not just a solo chain](https://medium.com/coinmonks/edgeware-a-multi-chain-reality-not-just-a-solo-chain-5769d95638c5) post.

![](https://commonwealth-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/0ca76080-c59c-4f10-8c3e-9fd35e8d73b5.1633265300054)

Despite the fact that people think we are completely aligned, it has also been challenging for us to align our visions because once again, we are trying to reconcile often competing design ideas.  

## Edgeware's limiting factors

We cannot change the distribution, we have the community we have, therefore we should be pragmatic about how our time should be spent and where Edgeware can offer a truly unique offering based on its foundations - technical, economic, cultural. 

It is unrealistic to think that we will get success with a solely ETH first value accrual model if we just copy/paste apps over to EDG. 

Picoswap may be useful, but it will not shift the dial. Sure, if we spray funds around enough, then we may come across a hit app, but this is something that cannot possibly be predicted and this approach comes at the expense of the DCR approach to building trust in the money. 

We should look instead at how Edgeware can offer the best of an ETH and DCR models, one that it can take the best of both and indeed of Substrate and the Parachain model of Substrate. 

## Edgeware's challenge 

**The Ethereum model offers a dimension oriented around breadth. **

It is a layered, hierarchical design - a single base platform chain and then a broad spread of tokens, each growing their own micro-economy and building connections to each other (money legos). 

**The Decred model offers a dimension oriented around depth. **

The design is about reinforcing the core, and focusing all energies into value accrual of the base token. 

In the same way, other projects that come over, need to materially expand the arena of possibility 

**The Substrate model enables versions of both**

1. Interoperability of parachains, like Ethereum's money legos. 
2. Application specific parachains w/ governance and treasury like Decred.


## **Edgeware's opportunity**

There is a third dimension which [@Ramsey](/edgeware/account/k44nJ5yAhFz3XHGeTPuKvegJ4GD1YCSVaPc7wj4miVL6epN) aluded to in his post and is where we have spend much of our time debating the role of Kabocha - an Edgeware incubated Parachain. 

Edgeware can birth new parachains via a 'chain factory' 

These app specific chains replace the ETH model, with a Substrate model. 

We fund R&D of parachains on Edgeware.

These parachains then bond either to an existing relay such as KSM or DOT, or we launch our own - after all a relay is still based on Substrate and involves a different selection of pallets and validators.

Each one of these Parachains is focused on L1 value accrual like Decred (which will need a new mechanic other than 21m coins / artificial scarcity), and in turn on ensuring EDG holders gain some share in the network in a manner similar to a L2 token airdrop. 

## Reaching true alignment

This model aligns us all - and gives us a chance to make our perceived weaknesses into strengths and acknowledges that all have a role to play. 

There are a number of proposals that are coming to Edgeware soon - including Kabocha, and all will be oriented around this chain factory model. 

The proposals come from projects from ETH looking to make a home on EDG and entirely new projects from teams outside crypto. The good thing is, it works for both. 

There is also an idea that I think can ensure value accrual to the base asset without relying on enforcing artificial scarcity of 21m coins as DCR does. 

## Summary 

The core disagreement comes from a misunderstanding of the 'platform' nature of Edgeware. 

We are are all therefore talking in slightly different languages.

We can solve this by going 'all-in' on Substrate in a way that benefits both an ETH platform mindset and a DCR platform mindset and provides Edgeware with a unique proposition in the Polkadot space that builds on its fair / wide distribution and on-chain gov experience. 

**We have a path to creating community monies that accrue direct value and an emergent layered structure - via a parachain factory model and it is this I believe we should focus our attention on. **

I haven't said anything about a technical committee, but since it's been brought up twice:

- Does the technical committee need to be implemented as a pallet?Wouldn't it make more sense for it to be an informal collective, like a multisig DAO on the EVM?
- That accomplishes the goal of recognizing technical members' input, while any on-chain action still needs to go through the normal coin voting process.
- I have other entrepreneurial focuses right now, and even if EDG has amazing upside my focus is on projects with shared values and principles of substance :)  If EDG is that, then great, if not, then there are plenty of other places for DAOs and governance experimentation


---

Addendum: we've said that Edgeware should be a "network of DAOs". Do we still believe in that vision? Is this thing about max decentralization opposed to that? Or is it not, and there is some coherent political structure that we are trying to create here?

Second addendum: I don't have an editor and these posts are largely written off the cuff, just wanted to mention that if it's helpful context

> Does the technical committee need to be implemented as a pallet?Wouldn't it make more sense for it to be an informal collective, like a multisig DAO on the EVM?

The main question is how these are selected without making it entirely subjective. 

My view - IF we had a technical committee it should emerge over time as we incubate parachains. Every launcher of a chain should be on the committee. 

> I have other entrepreneurial focuses right now, and even if EDG has amazing upside my focus is on projects with shared values and principles of substance :) 

Edgeware was originally articulated as a place for on-chain governance experiments. 

That was correct, other than the fact that **Edgeware itself is the experiment. **

Values and principles emerge over time. Don't forget we are still very early. 

People lack patience in this space, where massive returns are the short term view of 'success', this is not the only way to consider success.

> If EDG is that, then great, if not, then there are plenty of other places for DAOs and governance experimentation

You might be able to experiment with DAOs and governance, but EDG is the only place you can experiment with the Substrate chain factory model on top of a fair distribution.

Just following on from your addendum too:
> Addendum: we've said that Edgeware should be a "network of DAOs". Do we still believe in that vision? Is this thing about max decentralization opposed to that? Or is it not, and there is some coherent political structure that we are trying to create here? 

I absolutely believe this... but let's just dig in, when you say DAO we can mean a few things.

1. The chain itself and the all holder referendums 
2. A multisig that has funds deployed from a chain treasury 
3. A multisig that has funds deployed from members in return for a token / voting rights. 


1 and 2 are what we're doing right now on Edgeware.

3 is what ETH DAOs do. 

Let's get our definitions in order...

Hi Raymond,

Thanks for the thread this goes to the heart and core of Edgeware.

I will start at the end NOBODY OWNS EDGEWARE.
Whilst a technical committee might make things easier in the short term we cannot allow any potential for attack vectors.

The fact we are a DAO chain factory means that we should recognize the importance of decentralization. If we allow one group to control too much power Edgeware will fail.

I think you should view this as an opportunity not a problem and use your entrepreneurship and think outside the box for this solution.

As an entrepreneur myself I would be thinking about the extreme opportunity you have here with your technical talents. 

There is no reason you cannot achieve everything you want without a technical committee.

I also agree strongly. It is not sufficient that we author grants and bounties when we have a need, but retain someone to continue core development and to be accountable to inevitable unexpected challenges.

body:
I feel that this post is pretty much a summary of the last 8+ months of the current situation, you nailed it Ray. IMO the clear vision is certainly missing. All what I read on Discord channels are comments like "this is in pipeline", "there are tentative plans", "this will be announced after WAKO upgrade"etc...nothing specific and taking under consideration that ERUP 4 update is pending for quite some time I'm not expecting  straightforward answer anytime soon.

All problems were already named in the post above, I want to highlight  the one which is to me absolutely incomprehensible. How can non-technical people steer a wheel of technical strategy?! That's like asking your hairdresser to do a brain surgery to you.

Drew mentioned several times that Edgeware need to hire more CORE Devs, period. I do not remember who exactly was that but someone put an idea on a table to hire chain-contractors when CORE updates will be required. I'm sorry but what a nonsense! We need people who will work for the blockchain permanently and will be helping with the technical development...

Anyways, market cap is mirroring these difficulties quite precisely.

> How can non-technical people steer a wheel of technical strategy?! That's like asking your hairdresser to do a brain surgery to you. 

In the end, there should be an understanding of who does what, but the core advantage of Edgeware and indeed of any L1 DAO with chain treasury and governance is that its success is about bringing people with different skillsets together. 

This really orients back to the general issue of calling out 'builders' as some poorly defined category. It is all about context. 

In this example, you are absolutely right we need some core expertise, but if that core development talent is building features nobody uses and is not aligned with a broader path to involving more people, you get nowhere.

We need to join the dots and work together, not isolate groups.
